name: Low-dose doxepin (Silenor)
lead: Doxepin is a tricyclic compound first approved by the US FDA in 1969 as an antidepressant under the brand name Sinequan. A low-dose oral tablet, Silenor, was approved in 2010 for insomnia characterised by difficulty staying asleep.[1][9] A 5% topical cream is approved for itching in atopic dermatitis or lichen simplex chronicus.[1]

Its connection to appearance runs through sleep. People who sleep poorly often report looking tired, with dull skin and dark under-eye circles, and sleep is also the period when recovery from training takes place; a medicine that helps someone stay asleep through the night is used, in that chain, to support a rested look and more consistent training. This is the reasoning behind including a sleep medicine in a looks encyclopedia, and it is an indirect link rather than a cosmetic effect of the drug itself.

At the low strengths sold for insomnia, doxepin's sedating effect is attributed mainly to histamine H1 receptor antagonism.[1][2][9] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2017 guideline includes low-dose doxepin among its recommendations for sleep maintenance insomnia.[3] No study has examined it for appearance outcomes, and no looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.
infobox: Tricyclic; H1 antagonist at low doses

paras: Doxepin was discovered in Germany in 1963 and introduced in the United States as an antidepressant in 1969, marketed as Sinequan.[9][1] For decades it was used at antidepressant doses (tens to hundreds of milligrams), where inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake is considered to predominate.[1][9]

The low-dose product followed work showing that very small doses retain strong antihistamine action without much of the reuptake inhibition. The FDA label for Silenor is dated 17 March 2010, and the approved tablet strengths are 3 mg and 6 mg.[9][11]

Silenor is indicated for sleep maintenance insomnia in adults.[1][3][12] The label states that the supporting trials lasted up to three months and advises re-evaluating if insomnia persists after 7 to 10 days of use.[12] Higher-strength doxepin is used for depression and anxiety, where reuptake inhibition is considered to predominate.[1] Trials have also examined doxepin for urticaria and for uraemic itch, and the topical cream is approved for pruritus.[1][4][5]

According to Wikipedia's summary of the registration trials, low doses improved sleep maintenance and sleep duration, with weaker effects on the time taken to fall asleep, and studies of up to 12 weeks showed sustained effect without apparent tolerance or rebound insomnia on stopping.[9] It also reports that a 1 mg dose improved most sleep measures but not time awake after sleep onset, which is why the label strengths are 3 and 6 mg.[9]

Independent syntheses are more guarded about the size of the effect. A 2022 network meta-analysis, as summarised on Wikipedia, found a standardised mean difference versus placebo of 0.30 at four weeks with a confidence interval spanning no effect, and rated the certainty of evidence as very low.[9] A Cochrane review of antidepressants for insomnia examined doxepin among the drugs and noted that no antidepressant is licensed for insomnia and that evidence for efficacy is unclear.[10] The AASM guideline, by contrast, made a recommendation for low-dose doxepin for sleep maintenance.[3]

In the 28 to 85 day trials summarised on Wikipedia, somnolence or sedation occurred in 4% of placebo recipients, 6% at 3 mg and 9% at 6 mg, with nausea, upper respiratory infection and hypertension each reported at low single-digit rates.[9] The label's most common treatment-emergent reactions (2% or more and more common than placebo) were somnolence/sedation, nausea and upper respiratory tract infection.[12]

The US label carries warnings about complex sleep behaviours such as sleep-driving, about worsening depression and suicidal thinking, and about CNS-depressant effects that can impair alertness and coordination; it also notes poor neonatal adaptation risk after tricyclic exposure in pregnancy.[12] Reported effects of higher-dose doxepin include dry mouth, constipation and low blood pressure on standing; contraindications include use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and glaucoma or urinary retention conditions.[1] A study of the anticholinergic activity of medications used by older adults is the source for its anticholinergic burden at conventional doses, while sources describing the low-dose tablet report no clinically relevant anticholinergic effects at under 10 mg.[6][9] Genotype guidelines address CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 effects on tricyclic dosing.[7]

A 2011 Nature paper reported the structure of the human histamine H1 receptor bound to doxepin, which underpins its description as a potent H1 antagonist.[2] The Silenor label states that the mechanism of action in sleep maintenance is unclear but could be mediated through H1 antagonism.[12] Reviews of antidepressants and sleep describe how different agents alter sleep architecture in different ways depending on receptor profile.[14]

Phase 2 trial NCT00755495 enrolled 472 people with chronic insomnia to compare ramelteon and doxepin.[8] A registered phase 4 study in 52 healthy volunteers compared zolpidem, Silenor and placebo on arousability, balance and cognition.[13] The AASM guideline reviewed trials of low-dose doxepin in sleep maintenance.[3] The Medical Letter reviewed the registration evidence in 2010 and a 2025 review of insomnia treatment in older adults discusses where low-dose doxepin fits.[11][15] Other registered trials studied doxepin for uraemic pruritus and urticaria.[4][5] No studies were found on doxepin for appearance outcomes.
Low-dose doxepin is prescription-only in the US.[9] Silenor is the brand for the insomnia tablet, while Sinequan and, for the cream, Zonalon are other brand names.[9]

card.summary: A prescription low-dose tricyclic approved for sleep-maintenance insomnia; no appearance evidence.

quick.overview:
Low-dose doxepin (Silenor) is a prescription sleep medicine approved in 2010 for staying asleep. It is a tricyclic antidepressant sold at much lower strengths for this purpose.

No studies link it to appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: At low strengths it mainly blocks histamine H1 receptors, producing sedation; at antidepressant strengths reuptake inhibition predominates.
quick.risks: Reported effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation and blood pressure drops on standing. It is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and is Rx-only.

chain: Low-dose doxepin taken at bedtime on prescription
Fewer awakenings and longer sleep in people with sleep-maintenance insomnia
A more rested look and steadier training
angle.text: Low-dose doxepin is a prescription sleep-maintenance medicine. Better sleep is associated with how rested the face looks and with recovery between workouts, which is the route by which a sleep drug connects to appearance.
